bull.b: Royal Caribbean has rebuilt substantial earnings power after the pandemic, combining strong revenue expansion with robust gross, EBIT, and net margins. This profitability provides capacity to fund fleet and destination growth while supporting resilience across the next several quarters.

Record booking positions and accelerating future-sailing volumes indicate sustained customer demand rather than reliance only on close-in sales. Forward visibility can support pricing, occupancy, onboard spending, and more consistent revenue growth as additional capacity enters service.

The Sandals and Beaches partnership broadens Royal Caribbean beyond cruising into the Caribbean all-inclusive market, adding adult-only and family resort offerings. The wider platform may increase cross-selling, deepen guest relationships, and capture more of customers' annual vacation spending.

bear.b: Leverage has improved materially from post-pandemic levels but remains high for a cyclical travel company. Debt service and refinancing needs can restrict financial flexibility, increase sensitivity to demand downturns, and compete with fleet, destination, or resort investment for available cash.

Strong operating cash generation is not converting consistently into free cash flow, which was weak relative to reported earnings and declined sharply year over year. Continued volatility could limit internally funded growth and make debt reduction or shareholder returns less predictable.

Management expects 2027 yield growth to be weighted toward the second half because first-quarter performance faces structural pressure from dry-dock timing. This creates an identifiable near-term drag on revenue productivity and could make quarterly margins and earnings progression uneven.
